paras: The attempted lynching of Frank Smith took place in Ogden, Utah Territory, on the night of Saturday, 18 November 1882, when a party of men set out to lynch Smith, who was held in custody, accused of shooting a railroad brakeman, Patsy Jones. The men could not find the place where Smith was confined and disbanded; Jones later died, and Smith was reported held in the Penitentiary. No report gives the race of Smith or of Jones.

On Friday night, 17 November, friends of John Elvin, a Central Pacific switchman killed at the Ogden depot, were holding a wake over his body at the Omaha House on lower Fifth Street. According to the Ogden Herald, a young man who gave his name as Frank Smith came in and asked for a night's lodging, was refused, and quarreled with the watchers before being crowded out the door by Jones. The Ogden Pilot put the time at 12:15 and said that Smith, once outside, turned and fired through the glass door, the ball passing through Jones's right lung.

Smith went to the Keeney House at the depot, took a room and went to bed, where he was arrested, according to the Pilot by Kelley and Keyes. He was taken to Jones's bedside, and Jones "solemnly and repeatedly" identified him as the man who had fired.

On Saturday night a rumor spread that a party of men was out to lynch Smith. The Pilot reported that inquiry showed a number of men had formed an agreement to lynch him, about twenty in the Salt Lake copy of the item and 70 in the Eureka copy. Fifteen of them went around hunting for the place where Smith was confined, but, unable to find it, they disbanded.

Jones died on a Sunday night after the shooting and was buried the following Tuesday in the Ogden Cemetery. The report of his death, which named the accused "John Smith," said Smith was in the Penitentiary and likely to hang. No report of an arrest of the would-be lynchers, an inquest or a trial was found.

The lynching attempt is known from a single Ogden Pilot item, headed "Vigilantes," that a Salt Lake paper reprinted on 21 November and the Eureka Daily Sentinel in Nevada on 24 November. The Pilot did not condemn the men; it said such "cold blooded attempts to commit murder" would become less frequent once one or two assassins "of the Smith stripe are strung up."

The shooting itself drew wider notice, from the Ogden Herald's account calling Smith an "arrant coward" to a brief Salt Lake wire item in the Wheeling Register headed "Killed While Watching a Corpse," which did not mention a lynching party. None of the reports framed the case in racial terms.

The two copies of the Pilot item differ on how many men agreed to the lynching, "about twenty" in the Salt Lake paper and 70 in the Eureka paper, though both say fifteen searched. The accused was called Frank Smith in the first reports and John Smith in the report of Jones's death.

Smith was not killed: the men who agreed to lynch him for the shooting of Jones could not find where he was confined and disbanded (A2, A5); this was an attempted lynching, and no paper gives Smith's race.

The lynching attempt is known only from one Ogden Pilot item, reprinted in a Salt Lake paper and the Eureka Daily Sentinel (A2, A5); the shooting itself is reported independently by several papers (A1, A3, A4).
